title: Borders That Vanished Still Decide Who's Rich

lines: This is Germany's money map: how much each state produces per person.
Now watch what happens when we draw a border that was erased thirty-six years ago.
It fits almost perfectly.
Not one of the five eastern states produces as much per person as the poorest western state.
Germany is not alone. All over the world, borders that vanished long ago still show up in today's money.
Some are a hundred years old. One was built by Rome.
And one is a coastline from the age of dinosaurs, that you can still see from space.
So why do some dead borders keep deciding who is rich, while others fade away?
We will go back in time, one border at a time, each one older than the last.
For forty years, this fortified line split Germany in two: a market economy in the west, a communist one in the east.
In nineteen eighty-nine the Berlin Wall fell. A year later, the country was one again.
At first the gap was huge. In nineteen ninety-one, a full-time worker in the east earned less than half of a western wage.
Since then the east has caught up a lot. Thuringia's output per person, after inflation, has more than doubled.
But in twenty twenty-five, the five eastern states still produced only about seventy percent as much per person as the west.
And full-time workers there still earn about a fifth less.
In twenty twenty-five, the typical full-time worker in the east earned about forty-six thousand euros a year.
In the west, about fifty-five thousand.
Why so slow? Start with the head offices.
When the east opened up, almost no big company moved its headquarters there.
Today, not one company in Germany's top stock index is based in the five eastern states.
Only about sixteen of the country's five hundred largest firms are.
Head offices mean research jobs and high salaries. So young people followed them.
Since then, well over a million more people have moved from east to west than the other way.
Saxony-Anhalt has lost about a quarter of its people since nineteen ninety.
Output per worker in the east has climbed from about a third of the western level to about eighty-five percent.
Close, but not equal.
So a border can vanish from the map, and still sit inside every paycheck. Now let's go back a century.
For more than a hundred years, there was no Poland on the map.
Its land was split between three empires: Russia, Prussia and Austria.
Each empire ran its part differently. Prussia built factories and a dense web of railways.
Russia, in its part, built far fewer.
Russia also pressed hard on the Catholic Church. Austria, by contrast, let Poles run much of their own local government.
In nineteen eighteen, Poland was reborn and the borders disappeared.
So, a century later, is the old Prussian side still richer?
Economists Irena Grosfeld and Ekaterina Zhuravskaya checked, village by village, on both sides of the old lines.
Here is the surprise. Differences in income, education and corruption have disappeared.
What did not disappear were things built into the ground and into families.
The railways the empires laid are still denser on the old Prussian side.
And people on the old Russian side still go to church less, a trace of Russia's long pressure on the Church.
You may have seen viral maps where Polish elections follow the old border perfectly.
Careful: the researchers found that much of that split is a smooth slope across the country, not a sudden jump at the line.
Lesson one: money can cross a dead border. Railways and habits cross much more slowly.
The same year another empire died: the Habsburgs of Austria-Hungary.
Its old eastern edge now cuts through five countries: Poland, Ukraine, Romania, Serbia and Montenegro.
The Habsburgs were known for a slow but fairly honest bureaucracy: courts, police and paperwork that followed written rules.
A team led by economist Sascha Becker compared people living within two hundred kilometres of that line, inside the same country today.
On the old Habsburg side, people trust courts and police more.
And they are more likely to say they never pay bribes, by roughly five to seven percentage points.
The survey was taken in two thousand six, almost ninety years after the empire fell.
Business owners in a separate survey said the same: on the old Habsburg side, courts seem fairer.
And when the researchers moved the line a hundred kilometres either way, as a test, the effect vanished. It sits on the real border.
Lesson two: an empire can leave behind trust. Or the lack of it. Now let's go back almost two thousand years.
This is the Limes, the frontier of the Roman Empire across Germany: about five hundred fifty kilometres of wall, ditches and watchtowers.
Rome gave it up more than seventeen hundred years ago.
That makes it by far the oldest human border in this story.
Economist Fabian Wahl looked at Germany from space at night, and compared both sides of that line.
On the old Roman side, the lights are brighter: about five percent by the strictest method, and twenty percent or more by others.
Cities close to the line are about half again as big on the Roman side.
The reason is roads. Romans paved roads between their towns.
Later rulers kept using them, towns grew along them, and many became today's highways.
Roman towns like Mainz and Trier never stopped being important. Their bishops and markets kept them alive after Rome fell.
Lesson three: a road outlives the empire that built it. And our last border is not even human.
This dark curve across Alabama and Mississippi is visible from space.
It is called the Black Belt.
In the age of dinosaurs, more than sixty-six million years ago, the sea reached all the way up here.
Tiny plankton shells piled up on the sea floor and became chalk.
That chalk weathered into some of the richest soil in the South.
In the nineteenth century that soil made cotton, and cotton made Alabama one of the ten richest states.
That wealth was made by enslaved people.
By eighteen sixty, almost half of everyone in Alabama was enslaved, most of them on these black soils.
Slavery ended. But the land stayed with the plantation owners, and the soil wore out.
Today, nineteen of the twenty-four Black Belt counties are still in what the Census calls persistent poverty.
Poverty there averages about one person in four, against about one in seven in the rest of Alabama.
And only about half of adults there have a job or are looking for one, against nearly two in three across the United States.
These are the same counties the civil rights marchers crossed, from Selma to Montgomery.
The soil did not make people poor. What people built on it did.
But the line of that ancient coast still shows where.
Five dead borders. So why do some fade, and others refuse to die?
Look at what lasted. Railways in Poland. Roads in Germany. Trust in the Habsburg lands. Land and poverty in Alabama.
Things that are built into the ground, or passed down in families, stay.
Things that money can move, like wages and schools, slowly level out.
That is what happened to Poland's income gap. Germany is still in the middle of it.
None of this is destiny. These are averages, and the researchers test them with fake borders that show nothing.
But next time you see a strange line on a money map, ask what used to be there.
Because the past does not stay in history books. Sometimes it stays in the map.
Which ghost border runs through your country? Tell us in the comments.
